title: Exit Ticket
description: One question at the end of class tied directly to the day's objective. Read them the same day and open tomorrow with the misconception.
howTo: Post one question aligned to today's I-can statement on the board with three minutes left. Give students index cards or a slip of paper and ninety seconds of silence to respond. Collect at the door and sort into three piles — got it, close, missed — before you leave. Open tomorrow with a two-minute reteach that names the most common error from last night's stack.
sourceName: Doug Lemov, Teach Like a Champion

title: Hinge Question
description: A single multiple-choice question mid-lesson that reveals whether to move on or reteach. All students respond simultaneously (fingers, cards, or digital).
howTo: Write one multiple-choice question whose distractors each map to a common misconception. At the pivot point of the lesson, ask every student to answer at the same time using fingers 1-4, ABCD cards, or a digital poll. Read the room in five seconds: over 80% correct, move on; under 80%, reteach with the misconception named aloud. Never call for hands — the whole point is simultaneous data.

title: 4-Corners Response
description: Students physically move to the corner labeled with their answer, then defend it. Reveals reasoning, not just the answer.
howTo: Label each corner with a possible answer or stance (A/B/C/D or Strongly Agree → Strongly Disagree). Read the prompt and give students ten seconds of think time before they move. Once in corners, give each group ninety seconds to prepare a shared defense. Call on one voice per corner and let students switch corners if they hear a better argument.

title: Whiteboard Slates
description: Every student writes their answer on a personal whiteboard and holds it up on your signal. 100% response rate, instant data.
howTo: Pass out mini-whiteboards, markers, and erasers at the start of the period so setup does not cost lesson time. Ask a question, give the same think time to everyone, then use one clear signal ("show me") for all boards to go up at once. Scan the room quickly — you are looking for pattern errors, not individual grades. Name what you saw before students erase ("three of you wrote x = 4, let's see why that's close but wrong").
sourceName: Doug Lemov, Teach Like a Champion

title: Cold Call with Wait Time
description: No hands up; teacher calls on students after 3–7 seconds of think time. Everyone stays accountable for thinking.
howTo: Announce at the start of the year that hands stay down — you'll call on people. Ask the question, then give a clear 3-7 seconds of silence (count in your head). Call a name and use warm supportive tone; if the student is stuck, offer a scaffold or bounce to another student and return. Return to the first student later so the norm is "I will come back to you" — never "you're off the hook."
sourceName: Doug Lemov, Teach Like a Champion

title: Think-Pair-Share with Sampling
description: After the pair, sample 3–4 pairs by name for their partner's answer, not their own. Rewards listening.
howTo: Pose the question and give thirty seconds of silent think time — students jot a note. Then ninety seconds of pair talk where each partner explains their thinking once. When you sample, name a student and ask "what did your partner say?" — this forces active listening during the pair phase. Take three or four such samples before synthesizing on the board.

title: Two-Minute Paper
description: At the close, students write for two minutes on "What's the most important thing you learned?" and "What's still confusing?"
howTo: With three minutes left, put the two prompts on the board. Give students a half-sheet and two full minutes of silent writing — set a visible timer. Collect and sort into three quick piles that night: clear understanding, partial understanding, confusion. Open tomorrow by reading one anonymized "still confusing" and answering it.

title: Fist to Five
description: Confidence check: fist = lost, 5 = could teach it. Do it before independent practice, not as an exit.
howTo: After a mini-lesson and one guided example, ask students to close their eyes and show a fist-to-five for their confidence with the skill about to be practiced. Scan quickly and count. If more than a third show 0-2, do a second worked example before releasing to independent practice. Never grade or comment on individual ratings — the value is in the aggregate signal.

title: Muddiest Point
description: On an index card, students write the one part of the lesson that's still murky. Sort into 2–3 piles, address tomorrow.
howTo: In the last five minutes of class, pass out index cards. Ask, "What was the muddiest point in today's lesson?" — one sentence, no names. Sort them that afternoon into two or three thematic piles by misconception. Open tomorrow by naming the most common muddy point and reteaching it in five minutes before the new lesson.

title: Show Me
description: Students physically show their answer (fingers for a number, thumbs up/down/sideways, ABCD cards, gesture for equation type).
howTo: Establish the gesture set at the start of the year — fingers 1-4 for A-D, thumbs up/side/down for agree/unsure/disagree, hand shapes for equation types. Ask the question and give think time, then call "show me" and all students respond simultaneously. Scan for the pattern in under five seconds and name what you see. Use it three to five times per lesson so response becomes automatic.

title: Quick Quiz (5 questions)
description: Ungraded 5-item quiz once or twice a week on the last 3–5 lessons. Immediate review answers as a class. Tracks retention.
howTo: Once or twice a week, open class with a five-question quiz on skills from the last three to five lessons — no new content. Give students five minutes and keep it ungraded (or 100% completion credit only). Review answers immediately as a class with a hinge-question feel: which items showed pattern errors? Log the class average per item in a simple spreadsheet — the data drives next week's warm-ups.

title: Error Analysis
description: Show a wrong answer (real student work or fabricated). Pairs identify the mistake and rewrite. Teaches the metacognition of "why is this wrong."
howTo: Project one worked example with a specific error — a real anonymous student work sample or one you have written to expose a common misconception. Pairs get three minutes to identify the mistake, explain why it happens, and rewrite the correct step. Sample two or three pairs and lock in the fix. Save the samples in a running deck across the unit so students see error patterns over time.
sourceName: IES Practice Guide — Improving Mathematical Problem Solving

title: Standards-Aligned Check
description: Write one item every day tied to a priority standard's DOK level. Log a class % correct in a spreadsheet. Data drives tomorrow.
howTo: Pick one priority standard per week. Every day write one exit-slip item at the correct DOK level for that standard — not just recall. Grade the stack that day and log the class percent correct in a spreadsheet with the date and DOK level. When the class hits 80% two days in a row on a given DOK, move to the next level; when it stalls, reteach.
sourceName: Norman Webb, Depth of Knowledge framework

title: Learning Log
description: Students keep a running log of "I can" statements and self-rate mastery weekly with evidence. Great for conferences.
howTo: Give every student a small notebook or digital doc with a running list of the unit's "I can" statements. Every Friday, students spend five minutes self-rating each I-can 1-4 and adding one piece of evidence — a work sample number, a quiz score, a note. Use the logs to lead two-minute conferences during independent practice next week. At parent conferences, students pull up their own log and walk families through it.
sourceName: Hattie & Timperley, The Power of Feedback

title: Retrieval Practice Warm-Up
description: Every class opens with 3 questions from prior weeks (spaced). Ungraded, low stakes. Builds long-term retention.
howTo: Post three questions at the door every day — one from yesterday, one from last week, one from two weeks ago. Give students three minutes to attempt them from memory (no notes, no talking). Review answers together in two minutes. Keep it ungraded; the cognitive lift of pulling from memory is the point, not the score.
